Definition: Plants, rocks and other small things scattered over a terrain in many copies, such as trees, bushes, stones and grass.
One kind of foliage, such as one rock model. A terrain can use up to 16.
One placed rock, tree or tuft of grass. A copy has its own place, size and turn, but shares its asset's model.
A flat picture standing up on the ground, used instead of a model for things like grass. Its clear parts are cut away.
How much an asset grows at each place on the ground, from 0 (none) to 1 (its full density). The Foliage brush paints it.
How many copies grow on each square unit of ground where the asset's coverage is full.
How far from the camera copies are drawn. Copies farther away are skipped.
A simpler version of an asset, such as a plainer model or a flat card, drawn in place of the full one when the camera is far away.
How many pictures a game draws each second. A higher frame rate looks smoother.
Skipping things that can't be seen, such as things behind the camera or too far away, so the computer doesn't spend time drawing them.
The graphics processing unit: the part of the computer that draws pictures, many points at the same time.
The central processing unit: the part of the computer that runs the program, one step after another.
